metric_rationale: For each subject, the metric asks whether the option favored by the highest-validity discriminating expert was selected on more than half of trials, assigning 0.5 for an exact tie. It then reports the prevalence of subjects showing that directional pattern. TTB predicts above-chance agreement because the first discriminating cue determines every choice, whereas tallying predicts below-chance agreement because every designed trial has the opposing option winning the cue tally. Thresholding at the subject level exploits this sign reversal while reducing sensitivity to individual beta and epsilon values and to binomial trial noise. The A/B-swapped pairs ensure that the result cannot be generated merely by a response-side preference.

This is first-discriminating-cue choice accuracy. Every designed pair has an exactly tied tally, so Tallying predicts a tightly estimated value of 0.5. Take The Best instead favors the option identified by the first differing feature and predicts substantially greater than 0.5 alignment except at its highest noise levels. Pooling all 96 trials keeps the per-subject sampling variance low, while the A/B-reversed pairs balance the favored response side and therefore prevent a generic A/B response bias from creating the contrast.

This is the conflict-by-choice interaction targeted by the design: the probability of choosing the Expert-5 winner on exactly balanced trials minus that probability on 3-versus-1 trials. TTB uses Expert 5 first on every stimulus, so its subject-level beta and lapse parameters affect both conditions identically and cancel in the expected contrast, keeping between-subject parameter variance low. CGRDA predicts a negative contrast: on balanced trials its open recency gate favors the final Expert-6 endorsement, whereas on imbalanced trials the gate closes and integrated evidence favors Expert 5's option. The metric aligns A/B reversals to the cue-defined winner, uses all 96 observations, and is computed identically on pooled and single-subject data.

This metric is the proportion of subjects exhibiting a reliable cue-position crossover: their probability of selecting the Expert-5/TTB winner must be at least 0.12 higher when Expert 1 supports that winner than when Expert 1 opposes it. TTB predicts identical winner probabilities in the two conditions for every beta and epsilon, so its within-subject contrast is centered exactly at zero; the positive margin prevents ordinary binomial fluctuation from being counted as evidence. CGRDA predicts a sizable positive contrast because its strong primacy weighting lets an opposing first cue and its compact ally overturn the four-cue majority, whereas a supporting first cue reinforces the TTB winner. Computing the threshold within each subject removes response-side preferences and stable overall choice noisiness, while averaging bounded subject indicators yields a stable pooled scalar and remains well-defined on single-subject slices.

This is response-side-balanced adherence to Expert 1, the stable-order winner among the two equally valid highest-validity experts. It is computed identically for pooled data and individual subjects. TTB predicts consistently above-chance adherence because Expert 1 is the first discriminating cue on every trial, irrespective of the number or reliability of lower cues. DCSC instead cancels the opposing tied top anchors and lets the unanimous lower-cue coalition determine the choice, predicting below-chance Expert-1 adherence. Pooling all 96 trials yields a low-noise subject-level estimate, while the exact A/B reversals prevent a response-side bias from masquerading as cue adherence.

This is a within-subject crossover contrast. It measures how much more often the highest-validity cue's winner is selected when it faces exactly one opposing lower cue than when it faces a coalition of two or more lower cues. Take The Best predicts the same top-cue adherence probability in both conditions for every beta and epsilon, so its expected contrast is zero; differencing also cancels stable response sensitivity and lapse variation. DCSC predicts a large positive contrast: the top-cue option remains near or above chance against one opponent, whereas compensatory accumulation makes the opposing option strongly preferred for multi-cue coalitions. Pooling all 32 one-opponent and 64 multi-opponent observations yields low sampling variance, while coding choices relative to the top-cue winner makes the exact A/B reversals cancel response-side preferences.

The metric is the side-balanced difference in adherence to Expert 1 between trained diagnostic trials and control trials. It discards the first two presentations of each diagnostic stimulus so ADCG's anti-concurrence estimate has time to develop, while retaining 60 diagnostic observations per subject. TTB assigns the same choice probability to Expert 1's winner in both conditions, so its subject-level nuisance parameters beta and epsilon cancel in the contrast. ADCG instead predicts selectively reduced anchor adherence when Expert 5 has repeatedly opposed the anchor coalition, but not when the equally valid Expert 2 dissents only in the controls. Averaging separately over trials where the anchor favors A and B removes response-side bias; exact reversal pairs keep both cells well populated. The metric is not raw agreement with TTB, but a condition-specific transfer effect of accumulated cue-dependence experience.

This metric estimates the noise-corrected variance of Expert-1 adherence across all six invariant stimulus profiles, pooling each profile with its A/B reversal. TTB predicts one common adherence probability on every trial because Expert 1 always discriminates first; after correcting finite-trial Bernoulli variance, its expected score is exactly zero even when subjects differ greatly in beta or lapse rate. ADCG instead assigns profile-dependent choice probabilities because coalition size, dissent composition, redundancy, rarity, and gating differ across the six patterns. The metric uses all 96 trials rather than only the two target profiles or a late subset, substantially reducing subject-level sampling variance. It tests a broad quantitative consequence—stable stimulus-profile heterogeneity—rather than merely restating the advocated theory's specific rare-versus-common target contrast.

This metric measures the overall probability of following the uniquely 95%-valid expert when it is isolated against either concordant pair of 72%-valid experts. Unlike the failed outer-minus-middle contrast, it retains the large common level difference predicted for both target classes and pools 32 balanced target observations per subject. SCCI's sharp isolated-anchor restoration gate should produce a consistently high anchor-choice rate on every repetition. ADCG's minority-first gate is closed on these profiles because the earliest active cue belongs to the two-cue opposition; its choices therefore depend primarily on coalition comparison, including dissent amplification and comparatively weak or absent protection of the anchor. Pooling outer and middle targets reduces binomial and subject-level variability, while exact A/B reversals balance response-side bias.

This metric measures overall following of the 95%-valid anchor on the two profiles where Expert 3 supplies the design's most diagnostic opposition. It combines the compact diagnostic target with the builder profile in which Expert 3 is the sole dissenter against the other five cues, including the anchor. ADCG should produce relatively low anchor following: learned anti-concurrence disengages anchor protection on the compact profile, while distinctive-coalition amplification gives the singleton dissenter substantial influence on the second profile. SCCI instead strongly protects the isolated anchor on the compact profile and, on the singleton profile, statically accumulates the five-cue anchor coalition without singleton amplification because the anchor is not isolated. Pooling both A/B reversals and all eight repetitions yields 32 observations per subject, substantially reducing binary sampling variance relative to a late-only difference score.
